questions.q: What does a loss function do?
options: It stores the trained model on disk
It takes a prediction and the true label and returns a single number representing how wrong the prediction was
It splits data into training and test sets
It selects which features to use
questions.explain: A loss function quantifies the gap between a prediction and the true answer as one number, giving the training process something concrete to minimize.

questions.q: In the lesson's scikit-learn comparison, why is zero-one loss (which just counts right vs. wrong) not useful for actually training a model with gradient descent?
options: It always returns a negative number
It only works for regression, not classification
It gives no gradient (slope) to follow, since it's a flat step rather than a smooth curve
It is identical to log loss in every way
questions.explain: Zero-one loss jumps abruptly between right and wrong with no smooth slope in between, so gradient descent has no useful direction to follow from most points — which is why smoother losses like log loss or hinge loss are used for training instead.

questions.q: What does the "gradient" in gradient descent represent?
options: The total size of the training dataset
The final test accuracy of the model
The slope of the loss function with respect to each parameter — which direction increases or decreases the loss
The number of layers in a neural network
questions.explain: The gradient tells you, for each parameter, which direction and how steeply the loss changes — gradient descent uses this to know which way is "downhill."

questions.q: What typically happens if the learning rate is set far too large?
options: Training converges faster with no downside
The steps can overshoot the low point of the loss, sometimes bouncing around or getting worse instead of settling
The model becomes immune to overfitting
The loss function changes automatically
questions.explain: A learning rate that's too large causes each parameter update to overshoot the minimum, which can prevent the loss from ever settling down, sometimes making it worse with each step.

questions.q: In the scikit-learn loss-function comparison, what do all six loss curves agree on, even though they differ in the details?
options: They all equal zero everywhere
A clearly wrong prediction costs more loss than a clearly right one
They are all identical curves
None of them depend on the prediction at all
questions.explain: Despite ramping up differently in the middle, every loss function shown agrees on the basic shape: predictions far on the wrong side cost a high loss, and predictions far on the right side cost close to zero.
